recentItems.title: Yemeni forces launch counteroffensive against Houthis, vow to retake Sanaa
recentItems.description:
Yemen's government forces are locked in intense battles with Ansarullah Houthi fighters on several fronts, ranging from the Red Sea coast to roads leading to the capital Sanaa. The government has vowed to retake the capital, with Deputy Defence Minister Major-General Samir Al-Sabri saying the decision has been made to "retake Sanaa." Fighting has intensified in Taiz, al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Hodeidah, Marib and al-Dhalea, with government forces claiming advances while the Houthis say they have repelled offensives. The Houthis are pushing towards the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, while government forces seek to stretch Houthi positions across multiple fronts. 
The World Health Organization says at least 728 people have been killed or wounded since August 23, with more than 21,000 displaced from Taiz alone. 

Al Jazeera's Hamza Mohamed reports.

recentItems.title: More than 2,300 ISIL-linked women and children remain trapped in Syria's Roj camp
recentItems.description:
In northeastern Syria, more than 2,300 women and children are imprisoned in Roj camp as relatives of suspected ISIL fighters and people linked to the armed group. 
Government sources have told Al Jazeera that their home countries are deliberately ignoring them. Damascus wants to close the camp, but rights groups have called it a "ticking time bomb", where many detainees are vulnerable to the influence of a handful of women linked to ISIL. 
There are about 50 nationalities represented in the camp, including American, Swiss, British, Italian, Belgian, Turkish, Russian, Chinese and Bosnian. 
One woman from Sarajevo said: "We are full of the trauma. We lost any hope. We are just waiting to go home." The women interviewed have not been charged with a crime or given the opportunity to present their case in a court of law. 

Al Jazeera's Bernard Smith sent this exclusive report from Roj camp in northeastern Syria.

recentItems.title: How Silicon Valley giants are turning into war contractors | All Hail
recentItems.description:
The military-industrial complex - the deep ties between big wars and big industries - has evolved into a military-tech complex. Palantir, Anduril, Google and other tech giants are selling AI-powered, computer-guided weapons systems branded as “smart,” “safe” and “surgical”.

But behind the gloss lies a dangerous truth of escalation, instability and an increasingly rapidly evolving tech sector that sees big money in big wars.

Join Ali Rae in Episode One of All Hail the Military - a five-part series that reveals the systems, power and hidden complicities that sustain global militarism - and the profound impact it has on us all.

recentItems.title: Iran nuclear standoff: Analyst says Tehran feels the international scene is shifting
recentItems.description:
The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency is urging Iran to re-engage as the US, UK, France and Germany seek a resolution that could refer Tehran to the UN Security Council for failing to comply with nuclear reporting obligations. IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said it is "more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge" over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to up to 60 percent at facilities hit in US and Israeli attacks. Professor Cyrus Schayegh of the Geneva Graduate Institute told Al Jazeera that Iran is "unlikely" to engage on the nuclear front "unless and until the United States start to engage with Iran and a bunch of Arab Gulf countries as well in the Gulf itself." He said Iran feels that with the US midterm elections approaching and third parties such as Qatar and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization becoming more openly critical of Washington, "the international scene is somewhat moving their way." Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman has warned that Tehran will take "necessary measures" if the Western powers pursue the resolution. Schayegh added that the US is a "superpower in relative decline" and that the US-Iran war is "accelerating that decline."

recentItems.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks hit energy sites and wound 73
recentItems.description:
Saudi authorities say Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, officially known as Ansar Allah, have carried out attacks on energy facilities in the south of the kingdom, wounding at least 73 civilians, including women and children. 
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said the attacks hit civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, calling it a "dangerous escalation" and a "blatant violation" of Saudi sovereignty. 
He warned the coalition would take "all necessary operational measures". 
Saudi political analyst Khaled Batarfi told Al Jazeera the escalation is "too much" and expects the coalition to respond "eye for an eye". 
The attacks come as fighting intensifies in Yemen, where government-aligned forces have launched a counteroffensive against Houthi positions. 
The World Health Organization says 1,078 people have been killed or wounded since August 24, while more than 21,000 have been displaced since Thursday.

recentItems.title: Canada imposes up to 50 percent counter-tariffs on US goods as trade war escalates
recentItems.description:
Canada is imposing counter-tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 percent on nearly $20bn worth of US imports, matching US levies on Canadian goods including machinery, textiles and consumer products. The measures escalate a trade dispute that has strained one of the world's longest-standing trading relationships after talks on a new deal collapsed. The dispute began with Donald Trump's return to office, when he imposed tariffs on Canadian imports and threatened further action, while also raising the prospect of Canada becoming the 51st US state. Canada has responded with its own tariffs and is exploring alternative trading partners, including the European Union and China. Trump has also threatened Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier, saying it must build its aircraft in the US if it wants to operate there, after previously threatening a 50 percent tariff on Canadian-made aircraft. The latest escalation comes as Trump threatens further measures, while economists warn the financial impact could be greater for Canada. The dispute has also boosted support for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, with 73 percent backing his position and saying they are prepared to endure the economic pressure.

Al Jazeera's Alan Fisher reports from the White House.
Jennifer Hassum is the Executive Director at the Broadbent Institute; a Canadian Public Policy Think Tank. 
She says tariffs will impact both economies, because they are very closely linked.
